# The Design Matrix Defines the Question

RNA-seq software does not discover a scientific comparison from a count matrix.
The analyst encodes one through sample metadata, a design matrix, and a contrast.
For gene $g$ and sample $i$, a negative-binomial generalized linear model is

$$
Y_{gi}\sim\operatorname{NB}(\mu_{gi},\alpha_g),
\qquad
\log(\mu_{gi})=\log(s_i)+\mathbf x_i^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta_g.
$$

Here $s_i$ is an effective library-size factor, $\mathbf x_i$ is row $i$ of the
design matrix $\mathbf X$, and $\boldsymbol\beta_g$ contains gene-specific
coefficients. A differential-expression estimand is usually a linear function

$$
\boxed{
\theta_g=\mathbf c^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta_g,
}
$$

where $\mathbf c$ is a prespecified contrast vector. The fitted model produces
$\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_g$; the estimate is
$\widehat\theta_g=\mathbf c^{\mathsf T}\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_g$.

The coefficient names printed by software are coordinates chosen by a coding
scheme. The contrast is the scientific comparison. Changing the reference level
can change individual coefficients without changing fitted means or a contrast
that has been translated consistently.

# Begin with the Estimand and Experimental Unit

Before constructing $\mathbf X$, state:

- the target population, such as adults with a specified disease;
- the experimental unit, such as patient, animal, or independently treated
  culture;
- the expression scale, typically a ratio of conditional expected counts after
  defined normalization;
- the treatment or condition comparison and its direction;
- the time, tissue, genotype, batch, and covariate values over which the comparison
  is conditional or averaged.

For example, “treated versus control” is incomplete if treatment effects vary by
genotype. A precise estimand might be the log2 fold change for treatment versus
control among genotype B units at day 7, conditional on the modeled batch terms.

Reads, cells from one specimen, lanes, and genes are not independent biological
replicates. If treatment was randomized to animals, animals are the units that
support the treatment contrast. Technical replication can improve measurement,
but it does not increase the number of independent assignments. Repeated samples
from one person require donor blocking or another dependence-aware analysis.

# From Metadata to a Full-rank Matrix

Suppose eight independent samples are split between control and treatment and
balanced across two processing batches. With treatment coding and control and
batch 1 as reference levels, the design `~ batch + condition`

creates columns resembling

$$
\mathbf X=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & I(\text{batch 2}) & I(\text{treated})
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The mean model is

$$
\log(\mu_{gi})=\log(s_i)+\beta_{0g}
+\beta_{Bg}I(\text{batch 2})
+\beta_{Tg}I(\text{treated}).
$$

Under the no-interaction model, $\beta_{Tg}$ is the conditional natural-log fold
change for treated versus control at the same batch. The corresponding log2 fold
change is $\beta_{Tg}/\log(2)$. Including batch does not “normalize the counts”;
it adjusts the modeled mean comparison for an observed systematic variable.

The matrix must have full column rank for all coefficients to be uniquely
identified. If every treated sample is in batch 2 and every control is in batch
1, the batch and treatment columns are identical. No contrast or software option
can separate their effects. This is a design failure, not a numerical nuisance.

# Common Designs and Their Contrasts

## Several independent groups

For control, drug A, and drug B, a no-intercept cell-means design

$$
\log(\mu_{gi})=\log(s_i)
+\beta_{Cg}I(C)+\beta_{Ag}I(A)+\beta_{Bg}I(B)
$$

makes each coefficient a group log mean apart from the offset. Useful contrasts
include

| Question | Contrast weights for $(\beta_C,\beta_A,\beta_B)$ |
|---|---:|
| A versus control | $(-1,1,0)$ |
| B versus control | $(-1,0,1)$ |
| A versus B | $(0,1,-1)$ |
| average drug versus control | $(-1,1/2,1/2)$ |

The last row compares the equally weighted average of two log means with the
control log mean. It is not the log of an arithmetic average of expression on
the count scale. Contrast weights must be interpreted on the model's link scale.

## Paired or blocked samples

If the same donor contributes control and treated samples, a fixed-effect design
`~ donor + condition`

compares conditions within donor, removing stable donor-to-donor mean differences.
Each donor needs the relevant conditions for a within-donor contrast. Treating
the paired samples as independent discards design information and usually
misstates uncertainty.

This fixed-effect approach is practical when donors are blocks and the desired
condition effect is common. More complex repeated measures, missing visits, or
donor-specific slopes may require correlation-aware linear modeling, mixed
models, generalized estimating equations, or pseudobulk strategies appropriate
to the data hierarchy.

## Factorial designs and interactions

For genotype $G\in\{A,B\}$ and treatment $T\in\{0,1\}$,

$$
\eta_{gi}=\beta_{0g}+\beta_{Gg}I(G=B)
+\beta_{Tg}I(T=1)
+\beta_{GT,g}I(G=B)I(T=1).
$$

Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{treatment effect in genotype A} &= \beta_{Tg},\\
\text{treatment effect in genotype B} &= \beta_{Tg}+\beta_{GT,g},\\
\text{difference in treatment effects} &= \beta_{GT,g}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The interaction asks whether treatment effects differ by genotype. It is not a
test of treatment within genotype B by itself. Omitting the interaction imposes
one common log fold change. Including it without adequate samples in every
relevant cell can make estimates unstable or non-estimable.

## Time courses

Time may be represented as a factor for flexible visit-specific effects, as a
continuous linear trend, or by splines for a smooth nonlinear trajectory. These
choices define different estimands. A likelihood-ratio or quasi-likelihood
omnibus test can compare a full model containing condition-by-time terms with a
reduced model, while planned contrasts identify changes at particular times.

Repeated observations from the same unit remain correlated. A fixed donor block
does not automatically represent every temporal covariance pattern, and a simple
count GLM that treats all visits as independent can be anti-conservative.

# Estimability Is More Than Matrix Rank

A contrast $\mathbf c^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta_g$ is estimable when it is
determined by the fitted mean structure—equivalently, when $\mathbf c$ lies in
the row space of $\mathbf X$ for the chosen parameterization. Full column rank
makes every coefficient contrast estimable, but scientific support also requires
overlap and replication in the relevant cells.

Sparse data can create three distinct problems:

1. **Exact aliasing:** columns are linearly dependent, so coefficients are not
   uniquely defined.
2. **Near aliasing:** columns are almost dependent, producing large standard
   errors and sensitivity to a few samples.
3. **Extrapolation:** a mathematical contrast exists but relies on combinations
   of covariates scarcely represented in the data.

Check rank, condition-by-batch tables, factor levels, and sample counts before
fitting thousands of genes. Dropping a column merely to make software run changes
the model; it cannot create information absent from the design.

# Estimates, Tests, and Uncertainty

Let $\widehat{\mathbf V}_g$ be the estimated covariance matrix of
$\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_g$. Then

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\widehat\theta_g)
=\sqrt{\mathbf c^{\mathsf T}
\widehat{\mathbf V}_g\mathbf c}.
$$

A Wald statistic compares $\widehat\theta_g$ with a null value, often zero. A
likelihood-ratio test compares full and reduced models, and edgeR's
quasi-likelihood framework tests contrasts while incorporating moderated
quasi-likelihood uncertainty. Multi-degree-of-freedom tests answer omnibus
questions, whereas a one-degree-of-freedom contrast answers one directionally
specified comparison.

The test and the effect estimator need not use identical shrinkage. DESeq2 can
test an unshrunk coefficient and separately produce a shrunken log2 fold change
for ranking and visualization. A shrunken estimate should not be paired casually
with an interval or p-value derived for a different estimator.

For each gene, report the contrast estimate, its scale, uncertainty, and the
tested null. Across genes, control the false discovery rate for the declared
family. If many contrasts are searched and only the most favorable one is
reported, multiplicity extends across contrasts as well as genes.

# A Design-aware Non-executed Workflow

This R syntax is illustrative rather than executable in Quarto; the site's
publication workflow does not install R or Bioconductor packages.

```r
# Samples must be in exactly the same order as count-matrix columns.
stopifnot(identical(colnames(counts), rownames(samples)))

samples$condition <- relevel(factor(samples$condition), "control")
samples$batch <- factor(samples$batch)

design <- model.matrix(~ batch + condition, data = samples)
stopifnot(qr(design)$rank == ncol(design))
colnames(design)

# DESeq2: the name/contrast should be checked against resultsNames(dds).
dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(counts, samples, ~ batch + condition)
dds <- DESeq(dds)
resultsNames(dds)
res <- results(dds, contrast = c("condition", "treated", "control"))

# edgeR: explicit coefficient weights for the same comparison.
y <- DGEList(counts)
y <- calcNormFactors(y)
y <- estimateDisp(y, design, robust = TRUE)
fit <- glmQLFit(y, design, robust = TRUE)
contrast <- makeContrasts(conditiontreated, levels = design)
qlf <- glmQLFTest(fit, contrast = contrast)
```

Before accepting the output, verify coefficient names, the numerator and
denominator, the log base, and the sign using a gene with an obvious count
pattern. This catches reversed factor levels and malformed contrast vectors.

# Diagnostics and Sensitivity

| Question | Check | Consequence or response |
|---|---|---|
| Are counts and metadata aligned? | exact column-name and row-name match | stop; repair provenance before fitting |
| Is the matrix full rank? | QR rank, aliases, singular values | redefine only scientifically supported terms |
| Is the target supported by overlap? | samples per condition-by-batch-by-time cell | narrow the estimand or collect data |
| Are experimental units represented correctly? | donor IDs, pairing, repeated measures, technical replicates | block, aggregate, or use a dependence-aware method |
| Does a few units determine the effect? | count plots, residuals, Cook's distance, leave-one-unit-out fits | investigate and report sensitivity |
| Does coding alter the result? | refit under an equivalent parameterization | explicit contrasts should agree numerically |
| Is the variance model adequate? | dispersion/BCV plots and residual diagnostics | revise design, trend, robust settings, or method |

Sensitivity analyses should preserve the scientific question while varying
defensible analysis choices: normalization, nuisance covariates, interaction
structure, outlier policy, filtering, dispersion moderation, and effect-size
shrinkage. If alternative designs target different populations or covariate
averages, label them as different estimands rather than treating their disagreement
as mere numerical instability.

# Statistical and Biological Interpretation

Suppose a treatment contrast gives a log2 fold-change estimate of $1.2$ with a
95% interval from $0.5$ to $1.9$ and a false-discovery-rate adjusted p-value of
$0.01$. Statistically, under the fitted model and multiplicity procedure, the
data support higher conditional mean expression in the numerator group, with an
estimated fold change $2^{1.2}\approx2.30$.

This does not establish a cell-intrinsic mechanism. Bulk-tissue composition,
RNA quality, mapping ambiguity, an unmeasured batch, or selection of samples can
also change the gene-level mean. The comparison is causal only if treatment
assignment, adherence, interference, missingness, and the adjustment strategy
support that interpretation.

Biological interpretation should combine direction and magnitude with interval
width, baseline abundance, replicate consistency, relevant isoforms or cell
types, pathway context, assay validity, and independent validation. A tiny but
precise difference can be statistically convincing and biologically negligible;
a large uncertain estimate may motivate more replication rather than a definitive
claim.

# Reporting Checklist

For a reproducible differential-expression contrast, report:

1. experimental unit, biological replicates per relevant cell, and treatment or
   sampling structure;
2. count-generation and feature-filtering rules;
3. normalization factors and their assumptions;
4. complete design formula, factor reference levels, and blocking variables;
5. contrast in plain language and, for complex comparisons, its coefficient
   weights;
6. test, dispersion procedure, effect-shrinkage method, and software versions;
7. effect estimate, scale, uncertainty, p-value, and multiplicity adjustment;
8. rank, overlap, influence, residual, and sensitivity checks;
9. separate statistical and biological interpretations.

Saving the exact sample table, design matrix, and contrast vector is often more
useful than saving only a final gene list.

1. The design matrix defines the modeled means; the contrast defines the
   scientific comparison.
2. Coding coefficients depend on reference levels, whereas a correctly translated
   estimable contrast is invariant to full-rank reparameterization.
3. Aliasing, missing cells, and lack of biological replication are design
   limitations that software cannot repair.
4. Interactions make main effects conditional; planned contrasts should state the
   genotype, time, tissue, or covariate distribution to which they apply.
5. A statistically calibrated contrast is not automatically a biological or
   causal mechanism; experimental units, effect size, uncertainty, and sensitivity
   determine the scope of interpretation.
